> **Enhanced T-Test Analysis with Automatic Selection, Assumption Checking, and APA-Formatted Output**

## 🎯 Overview

`enhancedTtest` provides a comprehensive solution for t-test analysis with automatic test selection, comprehensive assumption checking, and publication-ready APA-formatted output. Say goodbye to manual test selection and formatting headaches!

### ✨ Key Features

| Feature | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| 🔬 **Complete Test Coverage** | One-sample, two-sample (independent), and paired t-tests |
| 🤖 **Automatic Selection** | Intelligently chooses parametric or non-parametric tests |
| ✅ **Assumption Checking** | Automatically tests normality and homogeneity of variance |
| 📊 **APA Formatting** | Publication-ready tables with proper formatting |
| 📤 **Export Capabilities** | Export to Word (.docx) and HTML with one line of code |
| 📈 **Effect Sizes** | Cohen's d, r, with interpretive labels |
| 📝 **Plain-Language Reporting** | Automatic APA-style interpretations |
| 🚀 **Batch Analysis** | Analyze multiple variables simultaneously |

### 📋 Supported Tests

| Scenario | Parametric | Non-Parametric |
|----------|------------|----------------|
| **One-Sample** | One-sample t-test | Wilcoxon signed-rank test |
| **Two-Sample (Independent)** | Two-sample t-test (equal variances) | Mann-Whitney U test |
| **Two-Sample (Unequal Variances)** | Welch's t-test | Mann-Whitney U test |
| **Paired** | Paired t-test | Wilcoxon signed-rank test (paired) |


## 🚀 Quick Start

### Basic Usage

```{r}
library(enhancedTtest)

# One-Sample T-Test
result <- complete_ttest(mtcars, mpg ~ 1, mu = 20)
print(result)

# Two-Sample T-Test
result <- complete_ttest(iris, Sepal.Length ~ Species)
print(result)

# Paired T-Test
result <- complete_ttest(paired_data, value ~ time, paired = TRUE)
print(result)
```

### Export to Word

```{r}
# Export APA-formatted table to Word
result <- complete_ttest(iris, Sepal.Length ~ Species, 
                        export_word = TRUE,
                        filename = "ttest_results.docx")
```


## 📊 Examples

### 1️⃣ One-Sample T-Test

Test if the mean mpg of cars is different from 20:

```{r}
library(enhancedTtest)

result <- complete_ttest(mtcars, mpg ~ 1, mu = 20)

# View results
print(result)

# Get APA-style interpretation
summary(result)

# Access components
result$method              # "One-sample t-test"
result$effect_size$value   # Cohen's d
result$apa_table           # APA-formatted table
```


### 2️⃣ Two-Sample T-Test

Compare Sepal.Length between two species:

```{r}
# Compare setosa vs versicolor
iris_subset <- subset(iris, Species %in% c("setosa", "versicolor"))
result <- complete_ttest(iris_subset, Sepal.Length ~ Species)

print(result)
```

With Automatic Test Selection:

```{r}
# Non-normal data triggers non-parametric test
set.seed(123)
non_normal_data <- data.frame(
  value = c(rnorm(30, 10, 2)^2, rnorm(30, 12, 2)^2),
  group = factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = 30))
)

result <- complete_ttest(non_normal_data, value ~ group)
# Automatically uses Mann-Whitney U test
print(result)
```


### 3️⃣ Paired T-Test

Before-and-after comparison:


```{r}
# Create paired data
set.seed(123)
before <- rnorm(30, 10, 2)
after <- before + rnorm(30, 1.5, 1)

paired_data <- data.frame(
  value = c(before, after),
  time = factor(rep(c("Before", "After"), each = 30))
)

result <- complete_ttest(paired_data, value ~ time, paired = TRUE)
print(result)

```

### 4️⃣ Batch Analysis (Multiple Variables)

Analyze multiple variables at once:

```{r}
# Define formulas for multiple variables
formulas <- list(
  Sepal.Length ~ Species,
  Sepal.Width ~ Species,
  Petal.Length ~ Species,
  Petal.Width ~ Species
)

# Create comprehensive report
create_complete_report(
  data = iris,
  formula_list = formulas,
  group_var = "Species",
  title = "Iris Flower Measurements Analysis",
  filename = "iris_report.docx"
)
```

### 5️⃣ Export Options

**Export to Word**

```{r}
# Method 1: Direct export
result <- complete_ttest(iris, Sepal.Length ~ Species, 
                        export_word = TRUE,
                        filename = "results.docx")

# Method 2: Export existing table
result <- complete_ttest(iris, Sepal.Length ~ Species)
export_apa_to_word(result$apa_table, "results.docx")

```

**Export to HTML**

```{r}
# Export results to HTML
result <- complete_ttest(iris, Sepal.Length ~ Species)
export_apa_to_html(result$apa_table, "results.html")

```

**Custom Report Generation**

```{r}
# Create a complete report with interpretations
result <- complete_ttest(iris, Sepal.Length ~ Species)

# Generate APA-style interpretation
interpretation <- generate_apa_interpretation(result)
cat(interpretation)
```

## 📋 APA-Formatted Output

The package automatically generates **APA-compliant statistical tables** that are ready for inclusion in research reports, theses, dissertations, journal manuscripts, and other academic documents.

### Example Table Output

| **Statistic**             | **Setosa (n = 50)** | **Versicolor (n = 50)** |     **Result** |
| ------------------------- | ------------------: | ----------------------: | -------------: |
| Sample Size (n)           |                  50 |                      50 |              — |
| Mean (M)                  |                5.01 |                    5.94 |              — |
| Standard Deviation (SD)   |                0.35 |                    0.52 |              — |
| Mean Difference           |                   — |                       — |          -0.93 |
| 95% Confidence Interval   |                   — |                       — | [-1.10, -0.76] |
| *t*-statistic             |                   — |                       — |         -10.52 |
| Degrees of Freedom (*df*) |                   — |                       — |          98.00 |
| *p*-value                 |                   — |                       — |      < .001*** |
| Effect Size (Cohen's *d*) |                   — |                       — |           2.10 |
| Effect Interpretation     |                   — |                       — |     Very Large |

## Table Features

* ✅ **APA 7th edition compliant**
* ✅ **Times New Roman font**
* ✅ **Proper borders and spacing**
* ✅ **Significance stars** (*, **, ***)
* ✅ **Italicized table titles**
* ✅ **Descriptive footnotes**
* ✅ **Effect size calculations and interpretations**
* ✅ **95% confidence intervals**
* ✅ **Standardized statistical notation**
* ✅ **Publication-ready formatting**

### Example APA Footnote

> **Note.** *p* < .05, **p* < .01, ***p* < .001. Cohen's *d* values of 0.20, 0.50, and 0.80 represent small, medium, and large effects, respectively.


### 🔬 Assumption Checking

The package automatically checks assumptions and selects appropriate tests:

```{r}
# Check assumptions explicitly
result <- complete_ttest(iris, Sepal.Length ~ Species)
print(result$assumptions)

# Output:
# $normality_passed
# [1] TRUE
# 
# $normality_p_values
# [1] 0.452 0.789
# 
# $variance_passed
# [1] FALSE
# 
# $variance_p_value
# [1] 0.023
# 
# $recommendations
# [1] "Consider Welch's t-test (doesn't assume equal variances)"
```


### Assumption Tests Performed

The package automatically performs the appropriate assumption checks based on the selected statistical test.

| **Test Type** | **Normality Test**         | **Homogeneity Test** |
| ------------- | -------------------------- | -------------------- |
| One-sample    | Shapiro-Wilk               | Not applicable       |
| Two-sample    | Shapiro-Wilk (per group)   | Levene's test        |
| Paired        | Shapiro-Wilk (differences) | Not applicable       |


## 📊 Effect Sizes

### Cohen's *d* (Parametric Tests)

For parametric *t*-tests, the package automatically calculates **Cohen's *d*** to quantify the magnitude of the observed effect, in addition to reporting statistical significance.

```{r}
result <- complete_ttest(iris, Sepal.Length ~ Species)
result$effect_size

# $value
# [1] 2.10
# 
# $name
# [1] "Cohen's d"
# 
# $interpretation
# [1] "Very Large"
```


| **Effect Size** | **Interpretation** |
| --------------: | ------------------ |
|          < 0.2  |	Negligible      
|            0.20 | Small              |
|            0.50 | Medium             |
|            0.80 | Large              |
|          ≥ 1.20 | Very Large         |

The package reports the effect size alongside the test statistic, *p*-value, and confidence interval so that users can distinguish **statistical significance from practical significance**.

### r (Non-Parametric Tests)

```{r}
# For non-parametric tests
result <- complete_ttest(non_normal_data, value ~ group)
result$effect_size

# $value
# [1] 0.45
# 
# $name
# [1] "r"
# 
# $interpretation
# [1] "Medium"
```

| **r Interpretation** | **Interpretation** |
| -------------------: | ------------------ |
|                < 0.1 | Negligible         |
|            0.1 – 0.3 | Small              |
|            0.3 – 0.5 | Medium             |
|                > 0.5 | Large              |


### Effect Size by Test Type

| **Statistical Test**            | **Effect Size**                           |
| ------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| One-sample *t*-test             | Cohen's *d*                               |
| Independent two-sample *t*-test | Cohen's *d* / Hedges' *g*                 |
| Paired *t*-test                 | Cohen's *d* for paired samples            |
| Mann-Whitney U                  | Rank-biserial correlation / Cliff's delta |
| Wilcoxon signed-rank            | Rank-biserial correlation                 |
| ANOVA                           | Eta squared (η²) / Omega squared (ω²)     |
| Kruskal-Wallis                  | Epsilon squared (ε²)                      |
| Pearson correlation             | *r*                                       |
| Spearman correlation            | ρ                                         |

### Why Effect Sizes Matter

A statistically significant result does not necessarily mean that the observed effect is practically important. Therefore, `AutoStatsR` reports an appropriate effect size whenever possible.

For example:

> *t*(98) = -10.52, *p* < .001, Cohen's *d* = 2.10

This tells the user not only that the difference is statistically significant, but also that the magnitude of the difference is **very large**.


## 🔬 Assumption-Based Test Selection

The package uses assumption checks as part of its decision-making process rather than simply running a test without evaluating the data.

A simplified decision process is:

```text
                    Identify Test Design
                           │
            ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
            │              │              │
       One-Sample      Two-Sample       Paired
            │              │              │
            ▼              ▼              ▼
      Normality        Normality       Normality
        Check            Check           Check
            │              │              │
            │         Homogeneity        │
            │            Check            │
            └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                           ▼
                  Evaluate Assumptions
                           │
              ┌────────────┴────────────┐
              │                         │
        Assumptions Met          Assumptions Violated
              │                         │
              ▼                         ▼
       Parametric Test          Non-Parametric /
                                 Robust Alternative
```

### Important Design Principle

`AutoStatsR` should **not automatically switch to a non-parametric test solely because a Shapiro-Wilk test produces a significant result**.

The package should consider the overall evidence, including:

* Sample size
* Distribution shape
* Q-Q plot diagnostics
* Presence of extreme outliers
* Independence of observations
* Homogeneity of variance
* Robustness of the selected parametric test
* Study design

The final output should explain **why a particular test was selected**, rather than simply reporting the result.

### Example Decision Output

```{text}
Test Selection
--------------
Study design: Independent two-sample comparison

Initial candidate:
  Independent two-sample t-test

Assumption assessment:
  Normality: Potential violation
  Homogeneity: Violated
  Outliers: None detected
  Sample sizes: Adequate

Decision:
  Welch's t-test selected

Reason:
  The groups show unequal variances. Welch's t-test
  provides a more appropriate comparison without
  assuming equal population variances.
```

This makes `AutoStatsR` more than a statistical calculator—it becomes an **explainable statistical decision-support tool**.


## 🛠️ Advanced Usage

### Customizing Test Behavior

`AutoStatsR` provides advanced options that allow users to customize how statistical tests are selected, assumptions are evaluated, and results are reported.

Users can override the package's automatic decisions when they have specific methodological requirements or prior knowledge about their data.

```{r}
# Specify alternative hypothesis
result <- complete_ttest(iris, Sepal.Length ~ Species, 
                        alternative = "greater")

# Force parametric test (skip automatic selection)
result <- complete_ttest(iris, Sepal.Length ~ Species, 
                        auto_select = FALSE)

# Custom mu for one-sample test
result <- complete_ttest(mtcars, mpg ~ 1, mu = 25)

# Custom page orientation
result <- complete_ttest(iris, Sepal.Length ~ Species,
                        export_word = TRUE,
                        orientation = "landscape")
```


**Working with the Results Object**


```{r}
result <- complete_ttest(iris, Sepal.Length ~ Species)

# Access raw test results
result$raw

# Access descriptive statistics
result$descriptive_stats

# Access APA table
result$apa_table

# Access assumption checks
result$assumptions

# Access effect size
result$effect_size

# Access method used
result$method

# Access interpretation
result$recommendation

```

### **Customizing APA Tables**

```{r}
# Create custom APA table with notes
result <- complete_ttest(iris, Sepal.Length ~ Species)
ft <- create_apa_vertical_table(
  desc_stats = result$descriptive_stats,
  raw_result = result$raw,
  effect_size = result$effect_size$value,
  var_name = "Sepal.Length",
  paired = FALSE,
  table_title = "Table 1. Custom Title Here",
  notes = "Note. Custom footnote here."
)

# Export custom table
export_apa_to_word(ft, "custom_results.docx")
```

### 📝 APA-Style Interpretation

The package generates plain-language interpretations:

```{r}
result <- complete_ttest(iris, Sepal.Length ~ Species)
generate_apa_interpretation(result)

# Output:
# "An independent-samples t-test was conducted to compare Sepal.Length 
# scores between setosa and versicolor groups. There was a statistically 
# significant difference between groups, t(98.00) = -10.52, p < .001, 
# d = 2.10 (Very Large)."
```

## 🤝 Contributing

We welcome contributions! Please see our contributing guide.

Development Setup

```{r}
# Clone the repository
# git clone https://github.com/yourusername/enhancedTtest.git
# cd enhancedTtest

# Install development dependencies
install.packages(c("devtools", "roxygen2", "testthat", "knitr"))

# Install the package
devtools::install()

# Run tests
devtools::test()

# Check the package
devtools::check()
```

### Code Style

* Follow the [tidyverse style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org/).
* Use `styler::style_pkg()` to format code consistently.
* Write **roxygen2** documentation for all exported and internal functions.
* Add unit tests for all new features and bug fixes.
* Ensure all tests pass before submitting a pull request.
* Keep functions focused, readable, and consistent with the existing package architecture.

### Reporting Issues

Please report bugs, unexpected behavior, documentation issues, and feature requests through the [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/yourusername/AutoStatsR/issues) page.

When reporting an issue, please include:

* A clear description of the problem.
* The expected behavior.
* The actual behavior.
* A minimal reproducible example, where possible.
* The version of `AutoStatsR` being used.
* Your R version and operating system.
* Any relevant error messages or warnings.
